Water Service Line Leak Repair in Sarasota, FL

The buried pipe between your water meter and your house is yours to fix. SRQ Leak Pros connects you with a local pro who can find the leak and repair the line with as little digging as possible.

Quick answer: Water service line leak repair in Sarasota fixes the underground pipe that carries water from your meter to your home. A pro confirms the leak with a meter and pressure test, pinpoints it with acoustic or tracer-gas tools, then repairs the section or replaces the line. Leaks on the house side of the meter are the owner's job.

A water service line is a simple pipe with a big job. It runs underground from the meter box near the street, under the lawn or driveway, and into your home at the main shut-off valve. In many Sarasota yards it is only a foot or two deep, laid in sand. When it cracks, water can flow into the soil for weeks before anyone sees a wet spot.

What a service line leak repair includes

A complete job covers more than patching a pipe. Ask the provider to confirm each step:

  • A meter test to prove water is leaving the system with every fixture off
  • An isolation test to show the leak is between the meter and the house
  • A pressure test on the line, with the reading shared with you
  • Pinpointing with acoustic listening, tracer gas or line locating
  • A call to Sunshine 811 before any digging
  • A spot repair, a section replacement or a full new line
  • Bedding sand and backfill around the repaired pipe
  • A final pressure test and a meter check after the repair
  • Restoration of sod, pavers or concrete, if quoted

Signs and causes of a service line leak

Most service line leaks give at least one clue. This table links each clue to its likely cause.

What you noticeLikely causeWhy it matters
Meter flow indicator moves with all water offA break or a loose fitting on the lineWater you pay for is soaking into the ground
Green, soggy strip across the lawnA crack along the pipe's pathThe leak can wash out bedding sand and grow
Water bubbling at the meter boxA leak at the meter connectionIt may be the utility's side; report it first
Low pressure in every fixtureA large break or a crushed pipeThe house may lose water if it gets worse
Sunken soil or a dip near the drivewayWater carrying sand awayIt can undermine concrete and walkways
Rusty or cloudy water at all tapsOld galvanized pipe failingThe whole line may be near the end of its life

Common causes in Sarasota include old galvanized or polybutylene pipe, tree roots near the line, shifting sandy soil, high water pressure, and damage from fence posts, irrigation work or landscaping.

Meter side or house side: who fixes it?

Ownership usually splits at the meter. The utility looks after the water main and the line up to its meter. The owner looks after everything on the customer side, from the meter outlet to the house.

Sarasota County's FAQ explains that its field "runners" check reported leaks and decide whether the problem is the county's or the customer's. The county looks after more than 104,000 service lines. In July 2026, county officials told ABC7 Sarasota that repairs and leak detection on private property are the homeowner's responsibility.

If water is coming up inside the meter box itself, report it to your utility before you call anyone else. City of Sarasota customers report leaks to City of Sarasota Utilities. For the full breakdown, read who is responsible for the water line from the street to the house.

How the repair works, step by step

  1. Confirm the leak. The pro reads the meter with all water off. Any movement means a leak somewhere.
  2. Isolate the line. Closing the main shut-off at the house splits the yard line from the indoor plumbing. If the meter still moves, the leak is in the service line.
  3. Locate the pipe. A transmitter and receiver trace where the line runs, which is often not a straight path.
  4. Pinpoint the leak. Ground microphones detect the hiss of escaping water. On quiet leaks, tracer gas is pushed into the drained line and a sensor finds it at the surface.
  5. Plan the fix. You get the options: a repair coupling on one spot, a new section, or a full replacement.
  6. Dig safely. After 811 marks other utilities, the pro opens a small hole at the leak.
  7. Repair and test. The pipe is fixed, pressure tested and inspected before backfill.
  8. Restore. The hole is filled with bedding sand and soil, and the surface is put back as agreed.

Detection tools and what each one does

Top-ranking local pages mention tools in passing. Knowing what each tool does helps you ask better questions.

Tool or methodWhat it findsBest for
Meter and flow indicator checkWhether any water is leavingThe first test on every job
Isolation testWhich section holds the leakYard vs. house vs. irrigation
Pressure gaugeA drop in line pressureConfirming a leak before digging
Line locatorThe path and depth of the pipeLines with no records
Acoustic ground microphoneThe sound of water escapingMetal and rigid pipe under soil
Tracer gasGas rising through soil from a leakQuiet leaks and plastic pipe
Infrared cameraTemperature change on the surfaceHot lines and wet slabs

Repair options compared

  • Spot repair. A repair coupling or clamp on one leak. Fast and low cost, but best when the rest of the pipe is sound.
  • Section replacement. A new length of pipe where the line keeps failing, such as under a driveway edge.
  • Full line replacement. A new line from meter to house. Often the right choice for polybutylene, galvanized steel or a line with several leaks. See water line replacement.
  • Trenchless install. A new line is pulled or bored under the yard from two small pits. Read about trenchless water line replacement.

DIY checks vs. calling a pro

You can safely do the first checks yourself. Read the meter with all water off, look for wet spots, and shut off the main valve to see if the meter stops. Call a pro when:

  • The meter still moves with the main shut-off closed
  • Water is surfacing in the yard or near the driveway
  • You see sinking soil or cracks in concrete near the line
  • Pressure has dropped across the whole house

Digging yourself is risky. Florida law requires a call to Sunshine 811 at least two full business days before any digging, so other buried lines can be marked.

Florida licensing and permit notes

Under Florida law, the plumbing contractor's scope covers installing and repairing water and sewer lines on private and public property, including the digging that goes with it. Ask the provider for a license number and verify it on the state DBPR license search. A full line replacement usually needs a permit and an inspection from the local building office.

Federal rules also require every water system to keep a service line inventory that includes the customer-owned part of the line. Sarasota County has asked owners to self-report what their private service line is made of.

Local note

Local note: service lines in Venice often run through sandy fill near a high water table, so leaks may never surface. In North Port, long front yards mean long service runs that are worth locating before any digging. Homes on Siesta Key face salt air and sandy soil that are hard on metal fittings.

Water Service Line Repair questions

How long does a water service line repair take?

A simple spot repair is often done in a few hours once the leak is found. A full replacement can take a day or more, plus time for a permit and an inspection.

Can I keep using water while the line is leaking?

Usually yes for a small leak, but every gallon goes through your meter. If the leak is large or pressure is falling, shut off the main valve and call for help.

Will my yard be dug up?

Not usually. Pinpointing tools narrow the leak to a small area, so only one small hole is needed. Trenchless options can avoid a long trench.

Does insurance pay for a service line leak?

Many homeowners policies exclude the pipe itself but may cover sudden damage it causes. Some policies offer service line coverage. Check your policy and talk with your agent.

Should I replace the whole line instead of repairing it?

If the line is polybutylene or galvanized, or has leaked more than once, replacement is often the better long-term choice. A sound line with one break can usually be repaired.

What if the leak is at the meter?

Water coming up inside the meter box may be on the utility's side. Report it to your water utility first so they can check their part.
